Although Prop. 2 would take a modest step toward loosening the constraints of the Gann Limit, the limit itself would remain in place and continue to artificially restrict (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/) policymakers’ ability to meet state residents’ needs and create an equitable California.
What Are the Implications of Continuing to Prohibit State Leaders from Reducing or Suspending Debt Payments During a Budget Emergency?
Prop. 2 would leave in place the rules that prevent state leaders from reducing or canceling required annual debt payments. 17 (javascript:void(0)) In contrast, under current law, required deposits into the rainy day fund can be reduced or suspended during a budget emergency — a flexibility that Prop. 2 would maintain. In other words, paying down debt would continue to be prioritized over using those funds to address a disaster or to meet Californians’ basic needs during tough budget years when state revenues are down.
Moreover, under Prop. 2, this prohibition on reducing or suspending debt payments would remain in place for an additional 10 years, through 2039-40, after which these payments would be optional. Under current law, debt payments are required through 2029-30, after which they become optional.
The current rules unreasonably constrain state leaders’ options when there is a budget deficit. As recently as 2025, for example, the state faced a $15 billion budget problem (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5079). However, state leaders could not pause the required debt payments, taking a potential budget-balancing tool off the table. As a result, additional budget “solutions,” like freezing Medi-Cal enrollment for certain immigrants and reducing payments to health care clinics, were enacted to close the budget gap, even as the debt payments went forward.
By failing to allow state leaders to reduce or suspend required debt payments, Prop. 2 misses an opportunity to create another budget-balancing tool that could help to close deficits without resorting to harmful cuts.
What Are the Implications of Maintaining the Current Definition of “Budget Emergency”?
Under Prop. 2, state leaders could continue to reduce or suspend a required deposit into the rainy day fund and/or withdraw funds to help address a budget emergency. Prop. 2 also maintains the current definition of a “budget emergency,” which reflects either 1) a disaster or extreme peril or 2) insufficient resources to meet a specified prior-year General Fund spending level.
The current definition of “budget emergency” leaves out federal funds. As such, it fails to recognize the impact of federal funding cuts on California’s ability to support vital public services. For example, H.R. 1, the 2025 federal budget reconciliation bill — the so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” signed into law by President Trump — slashed federal funding for basic needs to help offset the cost of tax breaks for the wealthy and profitable corporations.
Millions of Californians will lose health care and food assistance due to H.R. 1. Yet, these massive federal cuts to vital public services do not count as a “budget emergency.” As a result, state leaders cannot tap the rainy day fund to help mitigate — if only temporarily — the impact of these federal funding losses and reduce the harm that H.R. 1 is inflicting on Californians.
By failing to broaden the definition of a “budget emergency” to include federal funding losses, Prop. 2 misses an opportunity to help state leaders reduce the harm of substantial federal cuts to vital public services.

Although Prop. 2 would take a modest step toward loosening the constraints of the Gann Limit, the limit itself would remain in place and continue to artificially restrict (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/) policymakers’ ability to meet state residents’ needs and create an equitable California.
What Are the Implications of Continuing to Prohibit State Leaders from Reducing or Suspending Debt Payments During a Budget Emergency?
Prop. 2 would leave in place the rules that prevent state leaders from reducing or canceling required annual debt payments. 17 (javascript:void(0)) In contrast, under current law, required deposits into the rainy day fund can be reduced or suspended during a budget emergency — a flexibility that Prop. 2 would maintain. In other words, paying down debt would continue to be prioritized over using those funds to address a disaster or to meet Californians’ basic needs during tough budget years when state revenues are down.
Moreover, under Prop. 2, this prohibition on reducing or suspending debt payments would remain in place for an additional 10 years, through 2039-40, after which these payments would be optional. Under current law, debt payments are required through 2029-30, after which they become optional.
The current rules unreasonably constrain state leaders’ options when there is a budget deficit. As recently as 2025, for example, the state faced a $15 billion budget problem (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5079). However, state leaders could not pause the required debt payments, taking a potential budget-balancing tool off the table. As a result, additional budget “solutions,” like freezing Medi-Cal enrollment for certain immigrants and reducing payments to health care clinics, were enacted to close the budget gap, even as the debt payments went forward.
By failing to allow state leaders to reduce or suspend required debt payments, Prop. 2 misses an opportunity to create another budget-balancing tool that could help to close deficits without resorting to harmful cuts.
What Are the Implications of Maintaining the Current Definition of “Budget Emergency”?
Under Prop. 2, state leaders could continue to reduce or suspend a required deposit into the rainy day fund and/or withdraw funds to help address a budget emergency. Prop. 2 also maintains the current definition of a “budget emergency,” which reflects either 1) a disaster or extreme peril or 2) insufficient resources to meet a specified prior-year General Fund spending level.
The current definition of “budget emergency” leaves out federal funds. As such, it fails to recognize the impact of federal funding cuts on California’s ability to support vital public services. For example, H.R. 1, the 2025 federal budget reconciliation bill — the so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” signed into law by President Trump — slashed federal funding for basic needs to help offset the cost of tax breaks for the wealthy and profitable corporations.
Millions of Californians will lose health care and food assistance due to H.R. 1. Yet, these massive federal cuts to vital public services do not count as a “budget emergency.” As a result, state leaders cannot tap the rainy day fund to help mitigate — if only temporarily — the impact of these federal funding losses and reduce the harm that H.R. 1 is inflicting on Californians.
By failing to broaden the definition of a “budget emergency” to include federal funding losses, Prop. 2 misses an opportunity to help state leaders reduce the harm of substantial federal cuts to vital public services.

- The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office has argued the state should save considerably more. In an April 2025 report on a similar proposal, it called excluding reserve deposits from the spending limit reasonable. But it said this version falls short and recommended a cap of 50% by 2055.

- The budget Newsom signed in June suspended a $5.4 billion required reserve deposit. Prop 2 doesn't prevent that kind of suspension.
- A PPIC poll from October found 61% of likely voters in favor, with a sharp partisan split (85% of Democrats, 23% of Republicans).

**Rule of thumb:** Vote yes if you mainly want a bigger cushion for downturns and think the Gann limit penalizes saving. Vote no if you want the spending limit to keep forcing surpluses back to taxpayers, or you're wary of giving lawmakers more room to spend.

Election Day is Tuesday, November 3, 2026. The main sources are the official voter guide, the LAO's analysis and its April 2025 report, and PPIC's October 2026 survey.

content.text:
I won't pick yes or no for you on this one. Prop 2 turns on a values trade-off: how much to save in good years versus keeping surplus revenue under the spending limit so it goes back to taxpayers. Reasonable people land on both sides. Here's what I found so you can decide quickly.

**What it does:** It raises the rainy day fund cap from 10% to 20% of General Fund taxes, exempts deposits from the Gann spending limit until the money is withdrawn, captures more of large capital-gains windfalls, and extends required debt payments through 2040. It keeps the same budget-emergency test for suspending deposits, though it adds a procedural shortcut.

**Facts that bear on it:**
- The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office has argued the state should save considerably more. In an April 2025 report on a similar proposal, it called excluding reserve deposits from the spending limit reasonable. But it said this version falls short and recommended a cap of 50% by 2055.
- The state is about $27 billion under the Gann limit this year, so the rebate concern applies mainly to future boom years.
- The budget Newsom signed in June suspended a $5.4 billion required reserve deposit. Prop 2 doesn't prevent that kind of suspension.
- A PPIC poll from October found 61% of likely voters in favor, with a sharp partisan split (85% of Democrats, 23% of Republicans).

**Rule of thumb:** Vote yes if you mainly want a bigger cushion for downturns and think the Gann limit penalizes saving. Vote no if you want the spending limit to keep forcing surpluses back to taxpayers, or you're wary of giving lawmakers more room to spend.

Election Day is Tuesday, November 3, 2026. The main sources are the official voter guide, the LAO's analysis and its April 2025 report, and PPIC's October 2026 survey.

PROP

INCREASES STATE’S RAINY DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Increases California's Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns. Fiscal Impact : State budget reserves would be higher. Supporters : CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel Opponents : None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Vote yes on Proposition 2 to protect schools, healthcare, and public safety funding. Proposition 2 doubles the state's Rainy Day Fund, stops politicians from overspending when there is a budget surplus, and ensures education funding continues during economic downturns. It has bipartisan support from firefighters, hospitals, health clinics, and educators.
CON
Proposition 2 guarantees more spending, not savings, creating a loophole that makes taxpayer rebates less likely by excluding reserve deposits from California's constitutional spending limit. It provides no new funding for education, healthcare, or public safety. Vote No to protect taxpayer rebates and constitutional limits.

PROP
2
INCREASES STATE’S RAINY DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
THE STATE BUDGET
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state's public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state's low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
How Does the State Raise Revenue? The income tax is the state's largest tax. It pays for most spending from the General Fund. Other major taxes include the corporation tax and the sales tax. Much of the income tax is paid by high-income taxpayers, whose incomes often include gains from stocks and other investments.
State Revenues Are Unpredictable. State revenues go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because revenues depend on how the economy and stock market are doing. When things are going well, revenues can grow quickly. When things are going badly, like during a recession or a stock market crash, revenues can decline by tens of billions of dollars. During a bad recession or market crash, total revenue declines over a few years can equal 50 percent or more of annual General Fund revenues.
The State Must Meet Certain Budgeting Requirements Each Year. The State Constitution requires the Legislature to pass a balanced budget each year. This means the state cannot adopt a budget that spends more money than is available. In addition, the State Constitution limits how much tax revenue the state can spend. This limit is called the “state appropriations limit.” Certain kinds of spending—like infrastructure—do not count toward the limit. All other spending, including money put into reserves, does count toward the limit.
RESERVES
Reserves Allow the State to Maintain Spending When Revenues Decline. The state puts money into reserves when the economy is doing well. This means that money is saved instead of being spent on public programs during these periods of time. When the economy gets worse and revenues decline, the state uses reserves to help maintain spending on public programs. Reserves help the state avoid some spending cuts, tax increases, and borrowing to balance the budget. Currently, the state has about $20 billion in reserves that can be used for any public program.
State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the “Rainy Day Fund.” The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state's main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year. Money in the rainy day fund can be used for any state program. In addition, the state must put more money into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than normal. During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of the rainy day fund.
Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level. Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no longer required to make additional deposits. The money that would have gone into the rainy day fund instead must be spent on infrastructure (like highways and housing).
DEBT
The State Has Different Kinds of Debts. The state has more than $250 billion in debts. These include debt for infrastructure and pension and retiree health benefits earned by state employees. The state also sometimes borrows money from other state funds to help pay General Fund costs. State debts are repaid over time, usually according to a schedule or plan. Each year, the state makes payments toward its debts.
State Constitution Requires the State to Make Extra Debt Payments Toward Pension and Health Benefits. The State Constitution requires the state to make extra debt payments above those normally made each year. The amount of these extra debt payments is the same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. The state may only use these extra debt payments to pay down long-term pension and retiree health care debts. Making extra payments toward these debts saves the state money in the long run.
Extra Debt Payments Optional After 2030. The requirement for extra debt payments ends in 2030. After that, the Legislature and the Governor could decide to deposit the money for extra debt payments into the rainy day fund instead. Or, the Legislature and the Governor could make smaller extra debt payments and put the rest of the money into the rainy day fund.
PROPOSAL
Save More in the Rainy Day Fund. Proposition 2 requires the state to make deposits into the rainy day fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of 10 percent of General Fund taxes). In addition, the state would make even larger deposits in years when revenues from taxes on investment gains are very high, like when the stock market is booming.
Extend and Expand Extra Debt Payments. Proposition 2 also requires the state to make extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of through 2030). These debt payments would be the same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. In addition, the amount set aside for extra debt payments could be used for an expanded set of purposes. Specifically, these payments could be used to make required payments to schools and community colleges, repay borrowing from other state funds, and repay certain loans from the federal government.
Change How Rainy Day Fund Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. Deposits into the rainy day fund would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out.
Change How Other Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. The state has an account to set aside funds when revenues are surging. By setting these funds aside, the state can avoid overspending when revenue estimates are particularly uncertain. Under Proposition 2, deposits into this account also would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out. This exclusion could not be larger than 10 percent of General Fund taxes in each year.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Budget Reserves Would Be Higher. By continuing to require deposits into the rainy day fund until the balance reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes, the state would save more over time. In addition, by depositing more money when revenues are surging, the state likely would save more in the rainy day fund in certain years. More reserves would make balancing the budget somewhat easier when revenues decline.
Possibly More Debt Payments. By requiring the state to make extra debt payments through 2040, the state might make more debt payments than it would without Proposition 2.

2
INCREASES STATE’S RAINY DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 2
VOTE YES ON PROPOSITION 2 TO PROTECT SCHOOLS, HEALTHCARE, PUBLIC SAFETY AND CALIFORNIA'S FINANCIAL FUTURE.
California's Rainy Day Fund, established by voters in 2014, was built for exactly this moment: an economy that swung our state budget from a $100 billion surplus to a $50 billion deficit in just a few years.
Proposition 2 strengthens that fund, so schools, healthcare, and public safety don't pay the price for Sacramento's boom-and-bust budgeting. Voting YES on Proposition 2 will:
DOUBLE THE STATE'S RESERVE REQUIREMENT-from 10 to 20 percent of General Fund revenues-so California has a real cushion, not a token one, when the next downturn hits.
STOP SACRAMENTO POLITICIANS FROM OVERSPENDING-When tax revenues spike, this measure forces politicians to budget smarter by requiring the state to bank more of that windfall instead of committing it to new ongoing spending California can't sustain.
GUARANTEE EDUCATION FUNDING IS PROTECTED IN THE STATE CONSTITUTION, even as reserves grow.
INCREASE FINANCIAL SECURITY-As Washington moves to cut billions in health care and food assistance funding, this measure will ensure California is better prepared to absorb those losses without slashing the programs Californians depend on.
This is not a partisan idea. Republicans and Democrats in the state Legislature and Governor Gavin Newsom support Proposition 2.
California's own nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office has recommended that the state should be saving significantly more than current rules require. Proposition 2 follows that advice.
Please join the California Professional Firefighters, small business organizations, and former Health Secretary Xavier Becerra in supporting Proposition 2 because they see, firsthand, what happens when reserves run dry: healthcare clinics closed, schools defunded, essential services cut, and fire protection slashed.
Saving for a rainy day is what California families do. It's what California's state government should do too. Vote YES on Proposition 2-and make sure the next time the economy turns, California is ready.
Learn more at YesOnProp2.com .
Darrell Roberts , President
California Professional Firefighters
Jesse Gabriel , Chair
California State Assembly Budget Committee
Maria S. Salinas , CEO
Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 2
The supporters of Proposition 2 want you to believe this measure is about fiscal responsibility and protecting funding for education, public safety, and healthcare. Within 24 hours of introducing this measure, many of the same politicians who praised it as a way to build reserves also supported legislation to suspend more than $5 billion in required deposits into the state’s savings account. Proposition 2 asks Californians to double the size of the savings account while making it less likely that taxpayers will receive the rebates they are constitutionally owed.
PROP. 2 MAKES TAXPAYER REBATES LESS LIKELY
State revenues that exceed constitutional spending limits must be returned to taxpayers. Proposition 2 creates a loophole, allowing politicians to shift billions into reserve accounts that no longer count towards the spending limit, making your rebate far less likely.
PROP. 2 DOES NOT GUARANTEE ANY NEW FUNDING FOR HEALTHCARE, EDUCATION OR PUBLIC SAFETY
Supporters claim Prop. 2 will protect education, healthcare, and public safety. Currently, it doesn’t dedicate any new dollars to any of those priorities. Sacramento politicians will continue to decide how much to spend each year, not you. Prop. 2 only allows for politicians to spend more on pet projects.
Sacramento doesn’t need another budget gimmick or wasteful spending. It needs the discipline to live within the constitutional limits that voters have already approved.
Vote NO on Proposition 2.
David Tangipa , Vice Chair
Assembly Budget Committee
Carl DeMaio , Chairman
Reform California
Steven Choi , Vice Chair
Senate Elections and Constitutional Amendments Committee
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 2
Voting NO on Prop. 2 means more money in your pocket- and less wasteful spending!
PROP. 2 CREATES A SLUSH FUND FOR SACRAMENTO POLITICIANS
In 1978 California voters overwhelmingly voted to amend the state constitution to impose a spending limit on state politicians-and the politicians have hated that spending limit ever since. Prop. 2 allows the politicians to gut the voter-imposed spending limit. What the politicians dishonestly call a “rainy day fund” is actually a SLUSH FUND! Politicians can raid this new slush fund to feed their runaway spending habits.
PROP. 2 CANCELS YOUR TAX REBATE
California already has the highest taxes in the nation, but the state constitution requires that a tax rebate be provided to you when revenues exceed the spending limit. Prop. 2 creates loopholes and accounting gimmicks so politicians can eliminate any chance of you getting your tax rebate.
PROP. 2 ALLOWS FOR MORE WASTEFUL SPENDING
California’s state budget has grown by 76% since 2018-and the size of state government has mushroomed by 40% even after adjusting for inflation! Do you feel like you are getting 40% more services and benefits today than you did in 2018? Of course not! In fact, many core services to citizens have been gutted. We’re spending more, but getting less.
That’s because state politicians have diverted your tax dollars to boondoggle projects and no-bid contracts that reward their campaign contributors. Of the little money spent on important programs, too much of it is being lost because of fraud and wasteful spending. By eliminating the spending limit on politicians we will see even more wasteful spending.
PROP. 2 MAKES OUR BUDGET MORE VOLATILE
When times are good, the state is supposed to set money aside so families and businesses are not hit with tax increases, cuts to essential services, or budget chaos during the next economic downturn. Sacramento doesn’t need a new tool to save money. It needs the discipline to follow the rules already in place and stop spending money it doesn’t have. Prop. 2 makes our budget more volatile- putting us at greater risk of a financial crisis.
PROP. 2 IS OPPOSED BY TRUSTED BUDGET WATCHDOGS
Take a look at who is supporting Prop. 2: politicians who have repeatedly mismanaged our budget and special interests that get government contracts! Within 24 hours of putting it on the ballot, the politicians backing Prop. 2 voted to suspend more than $5 billion in required deposits into the state’s budget reserve. In contrast, opponents of Prop. 2 are government accountability and transparency watchdogs-including the Reform California and the Transparency Foundation. Californians do not need another budget gimmick dressed up as reform. We need honest budgeting, reform of wasteful spending, and a real spending limit to hold politicians accountable.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 2.
David Tangipa , Vice Chair
Assembly Budget Committee
Steven Choi , Vice Chair
Senate Elections and Constitutional Amendment Committee
Carl DeMaio , Chairman
Reform California
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 2
PROPOSITION 2 PROTECTS CALIFORNIANS FROM BOOM-AND-BUST BUDGETS
Opponents say the state needs “discipline,” not a new tool. But relying on their definition of “discipline” alone gave California a $100 billion surplus followed by a $50 billion deficit-exactly the boom-and-bust cycle Proposition 2 is designed to prevent. That instability, not this measure, is what leads to layoffs, healthcare cuts, slashed services, and tax hikes.
STOPS SACRAMENTO POLITICIANS FROM OVERSPENDING-Proposition 2 does not give Sacramento any new money to spend. On the contrary, it doubles the state’s reserve requirement and forces more savings-rather than new spending-when tax revenues spike.
PROTECTS SCHOOLS, PUBLIC SAFETY, AND HEALTHCARE-When the economy slows, Proposition 2 helps protect funding for schools, hospitals, health clinics, and public safety instead of placing them first in line for cuts. The theoretical “rebate” opponents refer to relies on a 50-year-old accounting gimmick that rewards spending instead of saving. Proposition 2 closes that loophole and mandates a real 20% Rainy Day Fund.
Don’t be fooled by those who call themselves “watchdogs.” California’s official nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office has recommended that the state expand the Rainy Day Fund to prevent boom-and-bust budget cycles. That’s why Proposition 2 is backed by the California Professional Firefighters, small business advocates, health clinics, hospitals, and education leaders-people who understand what happens when reserves run dry.
VOTE YES ON PROPOSITION 2- www.YesonProp2.com
Dr. Linda Darling-Hammond , President
California State Board of Education
Carmela Coyle , CEO
California Hospital Association
Francisco J. Silva , CEO
California Primary Care Association

### Summary
Proposition 2 was placed on the ballot by the California Legislature as Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 The amendment was introduced on June 25, 2026 and it passed the state Assembly by a vote of 59-8, with 12 not voting.
It passed the state Senate by a vote of 29-2, with nine not voting.
Proposition 2 on the November 2026 ballot would amend the State Constitution by changing California’s rainy day fund rules to build larger reserves and better protect public services during economic downturns and other budget emergencies.
Specifically, it would require the state to make deposits into the fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of the current 10 percent of General Fund taxes).
It would also expand the types of state debt that can be repaid with General Fund money set aside each year and require the extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of the current date of 2030).
In addition, Prop.
2 would change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending cap, or “Gann Limit,” making it easier to save more money when revenues are strong.
The Legislature placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot through Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20.

# PROP 2: Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund
###### Quick Facts
- **Official ballot title:** “Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund.”
(Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026).
The measure’s own name is the “Save for California’s Future Act.”
- **Type:** Legislatively referred constitutional amendment (a two-thirds vote of each house placed it on the ballot).

Analysis of Measure
Background
The State Budget
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state's public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state's low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
How Does the State Raise Revenue? The income tax is the state's largest tax. It pays for most spending from the General Fund. Other major taxes include the corporation tax and the sales tax. Much of the income tax is paid by high-income taxpayers, whose incomes often include gains from stocks and other investments.
State Revenues Are Unpredictable. State revenues go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because revenues depend on how the economy and stock market are doing. When things are going well, revenues can grow quickly. When things are going badly, like during a recession or a stock market crash, revenues can decline by tens of billions of dollars. During a bad recession or market crash, total revenue declines over a few years can equal 50 percent or more of annual General Fund revenues.
The State Must Meet Certain Budgeting Requirements Each Year. The State Constitution requires the Legislature to pass a balanced budget each year. This means the state cannot adopt a budget that spends more money than is available. In addition, the State Constitution limits how much tax revenue the state can spend. This limit is called the "state appropriations limit." Certain kinds of spending-like infrastructure-do not count toward the limit. All other spending, including money put into reserves, does count toward the limit.
Reserves
Reserves Allow the State to Maintain Spending When Revenues Decline. The state puts money into reserves when the economy is doing well. This means that money is saved instead of being spent on public programs during these periods of time. When the economy gets worse and revenues decline, the state uses reserves to help maintain spending on public programs. Reserves help the state avoid some spending cuts, tax increases, and borrowing to balance the budget. Currently, the state has about $20 billion in reserves that can be used for any public program.
State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the "Rainy Day Fund." The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state's main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year. Money in the rainy day fund can be used for any state program. In addition, the state must put more money into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than normal. During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of the rainy day fund.
Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level. Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no longer required to make additional deposits. The money that would have gone into the rainy day fund instead must be spent on infrastructure (like highways and housing).
Debt
The State Has Different Kinds of Debts. The state has more than $250 billion in debts. These include debt for infrastructure and pension and retiree health benefits earned by state employees. The state also sometimes borrows money from other state funds to help pay General Fund costs. State debts are repaid over time, usually according to a schedule or plan. Each year, the state makes payments toward its debts.
State Constitution Requires the State to Make Extra Debt Payments Toward Pension and Health Benefits. The State Constitution requires the state to make extra debt payments above those normally made each year. The amount of these extra debt payments is the same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. The state may only use these extra debt payments to pay down long-term pension and retiree health care debts. Making extra payments toward these debts saves the state money in the long run.
Extra Debt Payments Optional After 2030. The requirement for extra debt payments ends in 2030. After that, the Legislature and the Governor could decide to deposit the money for extra debt payments into the rainy day fund instead. Or, the Legislature and the Governor could make smaller extra debt payments and put the rest of the money into the rainy day fund.
Proposal
Save More in the Rainy Day Fund. Proposition 2 requires the state to make deposits into the rainy day fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of 10 percent of General Fund taxes). In addition, the state would make even larger deposits in years when revenues from taxes on investment gains are very high, like when the stock market is booming.
Extend and Expand Extra Debt Payments. Proposition 2 also requires the state to make extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of through 2030). These debt payments would be the same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. In addition, the amount set aside for extra debt payments could be used for an expanded set of purposes. Specifically, these payments could be used to make required payments to schools and community colleges, repay borrowing from other state funds, and repay certain loans from the federal government.
Change How Rainy Day Fund Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. Deposits into the rainy day fund would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out.
Change How Other Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. The state has an account to set aside funds when revenues are surging. By setting these funds aside, the state can avoid overspending when revenue estimates are particularly uncertain. Under Proposition 2, deposits into this account also would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out. This exclusion could not be larger than 10 percent of General Fund taxes in each year.
Fiscal Effects
Budget Reserves Would Be Higher. By continuing to require deposits into the rainy day fund until the balance reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes, the state would save more over time. In addition, by depositing more money when revenues are surging, the state likely would save more in the rainy day fund in certain years. More reserves would make balancing the budget somewhat easier when revenues decline.
Possibly More Debt Payments. By requiring the state to make extra debt payments through 2040, the state might make more debt payments than it would without Proposition 2.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
State budget reserves would be higher.
Ballot Label
Fiscal Impact : State budget reserves would be higher.

Critics say it would only allow state leaders to spend more in the future. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. The question Proposition 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/) poses to California voters is simple: Should the state be able to save more money when its economy is booming? The ballot measure, dubbed the Save for California’s Future Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca20), seeks to shore up California’s rainy day fund by allowing state lawmakers to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue — double the current ceiling of 10%. It would also require the state to save a bigger share of the gains when revenue is growing faster. Proponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers, say the state needs a bigger savings account to weather its volatile economy. Because California’s tax revenue depends so much on wealthy residents’ stock earnings, the state budget is often caught in a boom-or-bust cycle (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/) at the mercy of the market. In recent years, the state has seen robust tax revenue from an AI-fueled economy, which has helped state leaders avoid or delay painful cuts (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/gavin-newsom-final-budget-plan/) to social services even when they projected significant deficits. But economists have consistently warned the boom may not last, and the federal budget cuts to healthcare and welfare programs this year deepened that uncertainty. ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups (https://www.yesonprop2.com/#endorsements), including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce. “It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits,” wrote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/10/rainy-day-fund-california-proposition/) Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/jesse-gabriel-160858), an Encino Democrat, and Assembly Appropriations Vice Chair Josh Hoover (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/josh-hoover-165420), a Folsom Republican and the only GOP lawmaker to vote for the measure. Most Republican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend. “When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/279785#t=685&f=074f023444d682ecc1d857e24642a263) Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican. How long have we had a rainy day fund? Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst. In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-feb-10-me-dems10-story.htm) that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund. Sign up for free Δ But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments. In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it. “When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform. The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools. Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years. A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for. Bigger reserve = more to spend? Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending. “The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.” “Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.” In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times. “I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.” READ NEXT What to know about California’s other tax-the-rich measure: Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/) October 21, 2026 This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund.” (Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026). The measure’s own name is the “Save for California’s Future Act.”
Type: Legislatively referred constitutional amendment (a two-thirds vote of each house placed it on the ballot). It will pass with a simple majority.
A vote YES means: California would double the maximum size of its rainy-day fund from 10 percent to 20 percent of general fund tax revenues. It would also capture more money in years when capital-gains revenue spikes, extend mandatory extra debt payments through the 2039–40 fiscal year, and count rainy-day deposits against the Gann limit on state spending in the year the money is withdrawn and spent.
A vote NO means: The current rainy-day fund rules stay in place. The reserve remains capped at 10 percent of general fund tax revenues, and the requirement to split certain deposits between savings and extra debt payments expires after the 2029–30 fiscal year.
Sponsor/proponent: Legislative Democrats and Governor Gavin Newsome. Lead authors are Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Avelino Valencia and Senators Melissa Hurtado and John Laird, with support from Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and the governor’s administration.
On the ballot because: The Legislature passed ACA 20 by the required two-thirds margin on June 25, 2026. The Senate vote was twenty-nine to two and the Assembly fifty-nine to eight.
Full legal text: Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (2025–2026), California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)
LAO analysis: Proposition 2 (2026), Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=2&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 2 would enlarge California’s constitutional savings account, the Budget Stabilization Account, better known as the rainy-day fund. That fund already exists. Voters created its current form in 2014, and it is fed by automatic deposits each year. Proposition 2 does not create a new fund. It changes rules that govern how big the fund can grow, how fast it fills during good years, and how long the state keeps paying down old debts alongside it. Notably it also changes how deposits are treated under the Gann limit on state spending.
The headline change is the deposit cap. Today the state must keep making deposits until the rainy-day fund reaches 10 percent of general fund tax revenues. Once it hits that ceiling, extra money that would have gone into savings is instead spent on infrastructure. Proposition 2 raises the ceiling to 20 percent, so the state can keep saving until the fund is roughly twice as large as it can be under current law.
The second change targets boom years. California leans heavily on personal income taxes tied to capital gains, which rise and fall with the stock market. Current law captures capital-gains revenue above 8 percent of general fund tax revenues and steers it into savings and debt paydown. Proposition 2 keeps that trigger and adds a steeper tier on top of it. For the slice of capital-gains revenue above 10 percent of general fund tax revenues, the state would set aside 150 percent of that amount, pulling even more out of the biggest windfalls.
The third change is timing. Under a rule that began in 2015, half of these deposits go into the reserve and the other half pays down long-term debts such as pension and retiree-health obligations. That split is set to expire after the 2029–30 fiscal year. Proposition 2 extends it through the 2039–40 fiscal year. The eligible debts would include current and future school-funding settle-up payments owed under Proposition 98, money the general fund borrows from the state’s own special funds, and the state’s federal unemployment insurance loan, which stands at roughly $20 billion. The last two changes are new. Starting in 2027–28, deposits into the rainy-day fund would count against the state appropriations limit, known as the Gann limit, only when the money is withdrawn. Today they count when deposited.
2. The legal language
Full text: Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, “Save for California’s Future Act,” Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)
Key language:
“[T]he amount of a transfer to the Budget Stabilization Account … for any fiscal year shall not exceed an amount that would result in a balance in the account that, when the transfer is made, exceeds 20 percent of the amount of General Fund proceeds of taxes for the fiscal year.” The paragraphs cited are the required transfers, so voluntary deposits fall outside the cap.
On the steeper capture of capital-gains spikes, the amendment directs the state to set aside the sum of “the portion of the estimate … that is in excess of 8 percent, but not in excess of 10 percent” plus “150 percent of the portion of the estimate … in excess of 10 percent” of general fund proceeds of taxes.
On the Gann limit, the amendment provides that starting in the 2027–28 fiscal year, “transfers to the Budget Stabilization Account shall not constitute ‘appropriations subject to limitation’ for purposes of Article XIII B.” Money withdrawn later counts “in the fiscal year in which [it is] withdrawn.”
What it amends: Amends Sections 20 and 22 of Article XVI of the California Constitution, the article that governs state finance and the rainy-day fund. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal or alter it without returning to the voters.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Authored by Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Avelino Valencia and Senators Melissa Hurtado and John Laird, all Democrats, and championed by Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas with backing from the governor’s administration. It passed the legislature on largely party lines, with only two recorded Senate no votes.
What? Raises the rainy-day deposit cap from 10 percent to 20 percent of general fund tax revenues, captures 150 percent of the largest capital-gains spikes, extends the required extra debt payments from 2029–30 through 2039–40, and counts rainy-day deposits against the Gann limit only when the money is withdrawn.
Where? Statewide, written into Article XVI of the California Constitution.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If passed, the new deposit and Gann limit rules would apply starting in the 2027–28 fiscal year and the extended debt-paydown split would run through 2039–40.
Why? Proponents point to California’s volatile, top-heavy revenue base and the recurring deficits that follow every downturn. Their stated goal is to save more in good years so the state can protect schools, healthcare, and public safety without deep cuts or new taxes when revenues fall. The argument against calls the larger fund a “slush fund” and argues that moving deposits outside the Gann limit makes the taxpayer rebates it requires less likely.
4. Trade-offs
California’s revenue system is genuinely volatile, and that volatility is not a matter of opinion. The state relies heavily on personal income taxes from its highest earners, whose incomes rise and fall sharply with capital gains and the stock market. That design produces windfalls in boom years and sudden shortfalls in downturns. Reserves built under the 2014 rainy-day fund measurably softened the blow in the 2020 pandemic recession, and they were drawn down again as the state faced multibillion-dollar deficits in the years since, including an estimated $18 billion gap heading into 2026–27. A bigger fund that fills faster in boom years is a direct answer to a real and repeated problem.
But saving is not free. Every dollar the constitution steers into the reserve or toward extra debt payments is a dollar not available this year for schools, healthcare, child care, or tax relief. Raising the ceiling from 10 to 20 percent and capturing 150 percent of the biggest capital-gains spikes means more revenue is locked away by formula rather than appropriated through the annual budget.
Opponents object because of its effects on the Gann limit. Under the Gann limit, adopted by voters in 1979, revenue above the limit over two years must be split between taxpayer rebates and schools. Rainy-day deposits count as spending under the Gann limit today. Proposition 2 would stop counting them until they are withdrawn, which gives the state more room under the Gann limit in boom years and makes rebates less likely. The state had $27 billion of room under the Gann limit in 2026–27, so the change matters most in years when revenue surges past it.
Two further points deserve consideration. First, a larger cap does not guarantee the money will be there when a recession hits, because the constitution still lets the governor declare a budget emergency and the legislature can suspend or draw down deposits. A bigger fund raises the ceiling on saving, but it does not force the state to keep the money saved. Second, the most concrete and least disputed piece of the measure is the debt-paydown extension. Pension liabilities, retiree health obligations, and federal unemployment-insurance loans are real debts that accrue interest, and paying them down earlier has a measurable, defensible payoff regardless of where one lands on the reserve question. The reserve expansion is the contested part. The debt paydown is the part most budget analysts across the spectrum tend to endorse.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
A larger reserve gives the state a bigger cushion against California’s well-documented revenue swings, reducing the depth of cuts or the pressure for new taxes in a downturn.
Setting aside 150 percent of the largest capital-gains spikes targets the volatile money that has historically tempted the state into spending commitments it cannot sustain.
Counting deposits against the Gann limit only when they are withdrawn removes a penalty on saving. Under current rules, a deposit uses up room under the Gann limit the same way spending does.
The Legislative Analyst concludes reserves would be higher and that balancing the budget would be “somewhat easier when revenues decline.”
Potential risks
Money constitutionally directed into savings and debt is money not available now for schools, healthcare, and other services, a real opportunity cost in years when the budget is tight.
A higher cap does not lock the money in place. A governor-declared budget emergency still lets the legislature suspend deposits or draw the fund down, so the reserve may not be there when it is needed.
Formula-driven set-asides reduce the legislature’s year-to-year budget flexibility, shifting more spending decisions from elected officials to a constitutional formula.
Excluding deposits from the Gann limit makes its taxpayer rebates less likely in boom years. Withdrawals count when spent, but a surge can sit in reserves past the two-year window that triggers rebates.
The measure does not address the underlying structural imbalance between ongoing commitments and volatile revenues, so it manages the symptoms of volatility rather than the cause.
6. Open questions
How much larger would the reserve actually grow, and how many years of boom revenue would it take to approach the new 20 percent deposit cap?
In an average recession, would a doubled cap meaningfully change how deep the state's cuts have to be, or would the emergency-suspension rules blunt the benefit?
What current programs or tax choices would be crowded out in the near term by steering more revenue into savings and debt paydown?
How much of the extended debt payment would go to new paydown, and how much to settle-up payments and internal loans the state already owes?
In a year when revenue surges past the Gann limit, how much would the state move into the rainy-day fund and holding account, and how much smaller would taxpayer rebates be as a result?
How would the higher reserve interact with the Proposition 98 school-funding guarantee and the state’s constitutional spending limit in high-revenue years?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
California saves money in good years so it does not have to gut services in bad ones. Proposition 2 would roughly double how much the state can save and pull more from the biggest windfalls. Before you vote, ask whether a bigger locked-away reserve is worth the dollars it takes off the table for schools, healthcare, and other needs today.
A rainy-day fund only helps if the money is still there when the rain comes. This measure raises the ceiling on saving, but the state can still declare an emergency and spend down the fund. Does Proposition 2 build lasting discipline, or does it mostly raise a limit the legislature can waive when it wants to?

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

The question Proposition 2 poses to California voters is simple: Should the state be able to save more money when its economy is booming?

The ballot measure, dubbed the Save for California’s Future Act, seeks to shore up California’s rainy day fund by allowing state lawmakers to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue — double the current ceiling of 10%. 

It would also require the state to save a bigger share of the gains when revenue is growing faster. 

Proponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers, say the state needs a bigger savings account to weather its volatile economy. 

Because California’s tax revenue depends so much on wealthy residents’ stock earnings, the state budget is often caught in a boom-or-bust cycle at the mercy of the market. In recent years, the state has seen robust tax revenue from an AI-fueled economy, which has helped state leaders avoid or delay painful cuts to social services even when they projected significant deficits. But economists have consistently warned the boom may not last, and the federal budget cuts to healthcare and welfare programs this year deepened that uncertainty. 

Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups, including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce.

“It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits,” wrote Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel, an Encino Democrat, and Assembly Appropriations Vice Chair Josh Hoover, a Folsom Republican and the only GOP lawmaker to vote for the measure.

Most Republican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend.

“When they say we're here for fiscal responsibility, it's like the devil offering a Bible study. Don't buy it,” said Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican.

How long have we had a rainy day fund?

Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst.

In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund. 

But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees and delayed payments to schools and local governments. 

In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it.

“When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed stumping for the reform.

The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools. 

Under the law, state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years. 

A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for.

Bigger reserve = more to spend?

Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending.

“The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane, a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse that aims to “counter special interest influence.” 

“Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.”

In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times.

“I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.”

Will Californians vote to save more tax revenue in rainy day fund?

By Yue Stella Yu, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California’s booming stock market is bringing in billions of dollars in unexpected tax revenue.

Proposition 2, or the Save for California’s Future Act, aims to shore up the state’s rainy day fund by allowing state leaders to save up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue, up from the current ceiling of 10%. 

The state would also be required to save more when revenue is growing faster, and allow state lawmakers to use some of it to pay down California’s $20 billion in federal unemployment insurance debt. 

Supporters say saving more now would help the state weather a future economic downturn. 

California has been stuck in a boom-or-bust state budget cycle because its tax revenue depends heavily on wealthy residents’ stock market earnings. Some economists have warned the current economic boom may not last, and the state could face deeper budget uncertainties due to federal budget cuts and potential tax filing delays triggered by natural disasters.

Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic legislators spearheaded Prop. 2, which is also endorsed by labor unions, chambers of commerce and a coalition of advocates for healthcare, housing and transit. 

“If you don’t have a rainy day fund, then what happens is you get forced to contemplate cuts to core essential services,” said Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel, an Encino Democrat.

But opponents, including most Republican lawmakers, say saving more would only embolden legislators to spend more. The state should refund taxpayers during a good year, not set the money aside, they argue.

“When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican.

California leaders and voters have historically established reserves several times, but always quickly withdrew all the funds during budget crises. In 2014, voters approved a law that required the state to save more aggressively and made it harder to withdraw money. 

The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year for reserves and paying down debts. State lawmakers are allowed to withdraw up to half the balance from the reserves when the governor declares and the Legislature ratifies a budget emergency, unless they’ve already done that the previous year and the emergency remains. There are no limits on what lawmakers can spend the money on.

Prop. 2 would keep those rules and allow the state to save more. Critics say state leaders have too much leeway in spending the money. 

David Crane, a former economic adviser to former Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, said the rules let “governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.”

I'm checking the "$5 billion suspension" claim against the budget details. The enacted 2026-27 budget suspended a $5.4 billion true-up deposit for 2025-26, so the claim holds up. Opponents framed the vote as happening within 24 hours of the measure being introduced, which I'm still weighing.

I'm now looking at the June 2026 timing: the ACA 20 vote on June 25 and the budget signing on June 29, so "within 24 hours" is probably loose but the same-week framing holds. The Prop 2 emergency-suspension power is the key nuance, since the measure leaves those suspension rules in place.

I'm checking how the Gann limit fits in: LAO puts the state at about $27 billion of room under it for 2026-27, so the rebate requirement isn't close to binding right now. I'm weighing whether the CalTaxpayers claim about fewer rebates holds up given that headroom, since it only matters if revenues surge past the limit.

I'm going to look for more balanced views on the measure, from groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the California Republican Party, and Newsom, plus editorial boards. I also want to check whether the LAO has argued that the state should hold larger reserves than current rules require.

I'm checking the endorsements next, starting with the East Bay Times, which backs the measure, and then looking for where the LA Times, SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee, San Diego Union-Tribune, and OC Register stand. I want the opposing case in detail, especially the OC Register's "shell game" argument.

Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democrats in the state Legislature placed Proposition 2 on the November ballot to give government the ability to put more money into savings and create another option for leaders to avoid triggering taxpayer rebates during future budget surpluses.
The measure exempts deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters previously adopted through a series of ballot measures dating to the late 1970s, and increases the share of general fund tax revenue that can be put aside in reserves.

What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Under an existing state appropriations restraint, also known as the Gann Limit, lawmakers cannot spend more in the state budget than an amount determined by a formula that takes annual tax proceeds, changes to the population and cost of living into consideration.
Advertisement
Tax revenue above the limit must be divided between schools and refunds to taxpayers. More recent carve-outs in the law also allow leaders to direct excess funds to infrastructure and local government.
The limit applies to most other appropriations of tax revenue, including money that lawmakers tuck away into the “rainy day” fund and other reserves.
California voters also have capped the amount of money lawmakers can set aside in the rainy day fund at 10% of general fund proceeds in a given year.
The proposed changes would exempt deposits into the rainy day fund and a short-term reserve, called the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account, from the state appropriations limit. The cap on the rainy day fund would grow from 10% of general fund tax revenue to 20%.
In effect, the measure would allow the governor and the Legislature to put more money into budget reserves, creating another option to avoid triggering rebates.
Advertisement
For example, if the spending limit is $400 billion for the year, and revenue hits $410 billion, the measure would give lawmakers the option to deposit the $10 billion above the spending limit into the rainy day fund, direct the money to infrastructure or give it to local governments, instead of returning the funding to taxpayers and increasing funding for schools.
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Newsom, legislative Democrats and the California Democratic Party say the changes will allow the state to save more when the economy is growing and use the funds to lessen cuts to vital programs during a recession or stock market crash.
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Reform California, a political action committee started by state Sen. Carl DeMaio (R-San Diego), and legislative Republicans argue the proposal will allow Democrats to spend more money and hold on to revenue that otherwise would go back to taxpayers.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Since taking office, Newsom has argued that it doesn’t make sense for deposits into a savings account to count as spending under state law.
California’s budget revenue also is vulnerable to dramatic and at times unpredictable swings from year to year based on stock market activity. Newsom has said the state should have more flexibility during times of surplus to deposit money into the reserve accounts that lawmakers could then use during deficits to prevent big cuts to social services.
Advertisement
Statewide voters originally adopted the constitutional spending limit during an antitax wave in the late 1970s. Subsequent changes weakened the measure with exemptions to the limit for different kinds of appropriations, such as spending on infrastructure, and made it easier for lawmakers to avoid exceeding the limit and triggering rebates.
Revenue last exceeded the Gann Limit in 2021 when the pandemic left California with a predicted tax surplus of about $75 billion (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-05-10/gavin-newsom-new-stimulus-checks-californians-rent-assistance). As he campaigned against a failed recall, the governor set aside about $11.8 billion in cash rebates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-31/state-stimulus-checks-arrive-as-california-voters-cast-ballots-recall-election) for middle class and low-income residents under a program he called the “Golden State Stimulus.” The Newsom administration predicted a historic surplus of nearly $100 billion (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-05-13/california-budget-surplus-swells-to-97-billion-under-newsom-new-plan) the next year.

California Prop 2 guide: Expanded "Rainy Day Fund" would double amount saved for state budget reserves
Proposition 2 doubles the cap on California's rainy day fund to 20% of General Fund taxes, sets aside more of a capital gains surge, extends required debt payments to 2040 and stops counting deposits against the Gann spending limit until withdrawn.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 19, 2026
Link copied!
Copy failed!
California's Rainy Day Fund is going before voters as Proposition 2, which would let the state save up to 20% of its General Fund taxes for downturns.
Proposition 2 would double the cap on California's rainy day fund, the reserve the state draws on when a recession or stock market slump cuts tax revenue. Today the state must keep saving until the fund holds 10% of General Fund taxes.
Prop 2 raises that ceiling to 20%, requires larger deposits in years when capital gains revenue surges, and keeps the state making extra payments on its debts through 2040 instead of 2030. It also changes how savings count against the state's voter-approved spending limit, known as the Gann limit: deposits would no longer count when they are made, only when the money is taken out. The measure raises no taxes and spends no money. The Legislative Analyst's Office sums up its fiscal effect in six words: "State budget reserves would be higher."
California's Rainy Day Fund is capturing more of a capital gains surge under Proposition 2, which counts revenue above 10% of General Fund taxes at 150%. Prop 2, the Save for California's Future Act, is a legislative constitutional amendment (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/) that the Legislature placed on the ballot as ACA 20, by Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel, on June 25. It rewrites the rules voters adopted in 2014, also as Proposition 2, and is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/). PPIC's September survey found 60% of likely voters in favor and 39% opposed, one of the strongest results on the ballot. No campaign committee has registered on either side. This explainer covers what the measure changes, how the fund has been used since 2014, the spending-limit fight at the center of the opposition, the arguments and the polling.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) Proposition 2 doubles the cap on California's rainy day fund to 20% of General Fund taxes:
The rainy day fund's formal name is the Budget Stabilization Account. Voters created it in 2004 with Proposition 58 and gave it its current rules in 2014. Under those rules, the state sets aside 1.5% of General Fund revenues every year. Through 2029–30, half goes into the rainy day fund and half goes to paying down debts. The state must also set aside capital gains tax revenue above a threshold in boom years, split the same way. Once the fund reaches 10% of General Fund taxes, required deposits stop and the money that would have gone in must be spent on infrastructure.
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf) amends Article XVI, sections 20 and 22 of the California Constitution. Its central change is one number: the cap on required deposits rises from 10% to 20% of General Fund taxes. In its April 2025 report on the state's reserves, the Legislative Analyst's Office (https://www.lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) put the 10% cap at "about $21 billion." At that level of revenue, a 20% cap would be about $42 billion. The new rules apply from the 2027–28 fiscal year, and the money already in the fund stays there.
The 1.5% annual set-aside does not change. Neither do the rules for getting money out. The Governor still has to declare a budget emergency before deposits can be suspended or money withdrawn, and no more than half the fund can be withdrawn in a year unless money was also withdrawn the year before. The measure also says it does not change the minimum funding guarantee for schools under Proposition 98, and the separate school reserve keeps its own rules.
California's rainy day fund rules today and under Proposition 2 compared:
Rule California law today (Proposition 2 of 2014) Under Proposition 2 of 2026
Cap on required rainy day fund savings 10% of General Fund taxes. Required deposits above the cap must go to infrastructure. 20% of General Fund taxes. Required deposits above the cap still go to infrastructure.
Annual set-aside 1.5% of General Fund revenues, half to the rainy day fund and half to paying down debts Unchanged
Capital gains set-aside Capital gains tax revenue above 8% of General Fund taxes, counted dollar for dollar Revenue between 8% and 10% counted dollar for dollar; revenue above 10% counted at 150%
Required debt payments Required through 2029–30, then optional Required through 2039–40
Debts the payments can cover Pension and retiree health debts, budget loans outstanding on January 1, 2014, school funding owed as of July 1, 2014, and old mandate claims The same list without the 2014 cutoffs, plus federal loans to the state's unemployment fund and early payment of two costs now scheduled for later years: loans to a Medi-Cal provider payment fund and a school funding obligation under Education Code section 41206.04
State spending limit Rainy day fund deposits count toward the limit in the year they are made Deposits do not count when made; withdrawals count in the year they are taken out. The same treatment applies to the temporary surplus holding account, up to 10% of General Fund taxes a year.
